Why Charlotte generates MT demand

Charlotte anchors the Carolinas' energy engineering corridor — nuclear and gas generation fleets are engineered and supported from here, with turbine manufacturing, aviation MRO growth and a strong fabrication base in the surrounding counties.

Turbine components, boiler headers and structural welds take MT during outages — surface cracking at stub welds and attachment details is a known header mechanism.

Landing gear and engine components in martensitic steels are magnetic particle territory — high-strength parts where grinding cracks and fatigue must be found at overhaul.

In-process MT on fit-ups, tack repairs and completed structural welds catches surface defects while rework is cheap.

Rolls, couplings, hooks and lifting equipment in a steel plant are examined with MT on statutory and maintenance cycles.

What typically gets examined

In practice that means MT work across turbine and generator components, nuclear plant equipment within programme scope, fabricated structures and vessels, and aviation components — with scope set by the damage mechanisms each asset actually runs, not by a standard menu.

Certification and acceptance in Charlotte

Nuclear-adjacent work demands ASME Section XI thinking, 10 CFR 50 Appendix B quality programmes and personnel qualified under CP-189 rather than bare SNT-TC-1A — a materially higher documentation bar than commercial work carries.

Examinations themselves are performed to ASME Section V Article 7, ASTM E709 and E1444, and the ISO 9934 series, with acceptance from the governing construction code. The evidence chain — technician certification current on the day, instrument and reference block calibration, and the procedure revision in force — travels with every report, because that bundle is what an audit actually checks.
